headline: Shiraberu's senses “to investigate” and “to play an instrument” are probably a semantic loan from Middle Chinese 調.
Kaku is cognate with 掻く (“to scratch”): letters were originally scratched into wood.
Gakusei mixes go'on for the first character and kan'on for the second.
Kuro belongs to a root *kur that also reaches 暗い (kurai, “dark”) and 蔵 (kura).
Zenbu is borrowed from Middle Chinese 全部.
Raigetsu is 来 (rai-, “coming..., next...”) plus 月 (getsu, “month”).
Shitsumon is literally “quality + ask” in Middle Chinese, and is first attested in 1771.
Ocha is a compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 茶 (cha, “tea”).
Yūbinkyoku is 郵便 (yūbin, “postal service”) plus 局 (-kyoku, “office”).
Saki is cognate with 崎 (saki, “peninsula, cape”).
Yō is from Middle Chinese 用 (MC yowngH).
Zasshi is said to have been coined as a translation of English magazine, by the publisher of Seiyō Zasshi in 1867.
Ki is from Middle Chinese 氣, the kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.
Omou has two main theories; one has it cognate with 面 (omo, “face”).
Kami was kanpi: a sporadic change turned the mb sound into m, and Ainu borrowed it as kampi.
Ao may have been sawo before it was awo, but the source says the leading s is unclear.
Haru went /paru/ → /ɸaru/ → /haru/ from Old Japanese.
Hen went /pen/ → /fen/ → /hen/, from Middle Chinese 邊 (“edge; margin, border; nearby”).
Hajimete is from 始めて (hajimete), the conjunctive form of the verb 始める (hajimeru, “to begin, to start”).
Kumori is the stem form of the verb 曇る (kumoru, “to become cloudy”).
Oboeru comes ultimately from 思う (omou, “to think”), by a nine-step sound path starting at omopu.
Okiru descends from Old Japanese 起く (oku), from Proto-Japonic *əku.
Kinu is possibly cognate with Chinese 絹 (juàn, “silk”), via early borrowing.
Omoi is the attributive form of Early Middle Japanese 重し (omoshi), with the medial k fallen out.
Nomimono is 飲み (nomi, the stem of the verb 飲む) plus 物 (-mono, “thing”).
Otona appears in sources from the Heian period, from Old Japanese.
Tokidoki is a reduplication of 時 (toki, “time”), with rendaku.
Tomaru is inherited from Old Japanese, and a doublet of 泊まる (tomaru).
Atsui for hot objects is cognate with 暑い, the one used for hot weather.
Minasan is 皆 (mina, “everybody, everyone”) plus さん (-san), used when addressing a group.
